These pages contain lecture notes, examples, exercises, and supplementary
material for *Mathematics in the Modern World*.

::: {.callout-note title="Curricular basis and intended audience"}
The scope and organisation of these lecture notes follow the framework for
*Mathematics in the Modern World* set out by the Philippine
Commission on Higher Education (CHED) in
CHED Memorandum Order No. 20, series of 2013,
*General Education Curriculum: Holistic Understandings, Intellectual and Civic
Competencies*. CHED describes the course as addressing the nature of
mathematics, its practical, intellectual, and aesthetic dimensions, and the
application of mathematical tools in daily life.

The notes are written primarily for the BS Biology students whom I teach.
Whenever practicable, the discussion uses examples drawn from biology,
ecology, health, data analysis, and other situations that students may
encounter in their studies and subsequent work. The course also considers
less obvious applications: part of learning mathematics in the modern world
is recognising its presence in problems and decisions that may not initially
appear mathematical.

These independently prepared lecture notes are designed to support
*Mathematics in the Modern World* and are aligned with the course framework
established by CHED. They are personal teaching materials and should not be
understood as an official publication of Bulacan State University or CHED.
:::

## House rules

1. **Printed notes are available if you need them.** If you do not own, or do
   not have reliable access to, a laptop or mobile device, please approach me
   after class or during consultation hours. You do not need to explain your
   circumstances; I will provide printed copies of the relevant course notes
   free of charge.

2. **Attend regularly and arrive on time.** Consistent attendance is expected
   because much of the learning will take place through explanation,
   discussion, and guided work in class. Attendance will contribute to the
   final mark in accordance with the course syllabus and university policy.

   The course notes provide a general guide to what we intend to discuss, not
   an inflexible transcript of every class meeting. Depending on the time
   available, the pace of the class, and the questions that arise, I may
   change the order of presentation, supplement the notes with another
   example, modify a discussion, or omit a portion that we cannot cover
   responsibly. It is therefore important to **attend class** so that you know
   what was actually covered and what emphasis was placed on it. Any change
   affecting examinable material will be announced clearly; you will not be
   assessed on a topic that was added without notice.

3. **Participate and ask questions.** Questions are an important part of
   learning, and students are strongly encouraged to raise them in class.
   Consultation hours will be announced once the teaching timetable has been
   finalised. These meetings are suitable for questions requiring a longer
   discussion, including questions that go beyond the formal curriculum. This
   allows us to explore them properly while keeping class meetings focused on
   the material that everyone needs to learn. You may also send
   course-related questions or inquiries by email; the course email address is
   provided in the Logistics section above.

4. **Do not assume that biology contains little mathematics.** Modern biology
   uses mathematics to describe population growth, inheritance, epidemics,
   ecological networks, experimental uncertainty, medical images, and the
   behaviour of complex biological systems. A particularly striking example is
   the [2024 Nobel Prize in
   Chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/press-release/):
   half recognised computational protein design, while the other half
   recognised protein-structure prediction—the work associated with
   AlphaFold2. Both achievements brought biological knowledge together with
   computation, statistics, and mathematical reasoning.

   ::: {.callout-note title="A case in point: mathematics and biology"}
   My own BSc Mathematics thesis is a case in point. Although it is a
   mathematics project, it is grounded in a biological and medical setting:
   photographs of the retina at the back of the eye. Such images are used when
   assessing conditions including [diabetic
   retinopathy](https://www.who.int/europe/news/item/13-11-2020-who-europe-is-focusing-on-eye-screening-for-people-with-diabetes),
   in which diabetes damages blood vessels in the retina and can ultimately
   cause vision loss or blindness. I studied how computational topology can
   turn the connected components and loops appearing across a retinal image
   into numerical summaries, and whether those summaries remain reliable when
   the image is rotated, blurred, rescaled, or affected by noise. The project
   therefore brings together topology, computation, medical imaging, and the
   practical problem of retinal diagnosis. An expanded, self-study treatment
   is available in the [Topological Data Analysis
   section](/computational-topology/), while the complete project repository is
   available at
   [reyjosephnieto/ph](https://github.com/reyjosephnieto/ph). These links are
   included for curious readers; the mathematics required to study the project
   in detail lies well beyond the scope of this course.

   :::

   This course will not require students to train artificial neural networks.
   Its purpose is to develop the habits needed to recognise quantitative
   structure, interpret evidence, and reason carefully about unfamiliar
   problems. Those habits are useful in everyday decision-making and can be
   especially valuable to students who later pursue advanced study in biology,
   medicine, or related fields.

5. **Be present and considerate.** I am not interested in teaching through
   fear; there is no educational value in intimidating students, and I am
   probably more approachable than you may initially think. In return, I
   expect everyone, as adults, to take responsibility for maintaining a
   respectful learning environment. Please do not hold side conversations
   while someone is speaking.

   Electronic devices should be put away during class unless I have asked you
   to use one for a learning activity or an approved accessibility need
   requires it. This is not about feeding the instructor's ego. It is about
   giving yourself and those around you the attention needed to understand,
   question, and retain the material. I aim to choose topics that occasionally
   produce a genuine *“Wow, talaga?”* response; that moment of discovery is
   much harder to reach when our attention is divided between the lesson and a
   screen.

6. **Bring a notebook and a pen.** Since electronic devices will ordinarily
   remain put away, come prepared to take handwritten notes. Avoid trying to
   record the lecture word for word. Instead, use brief bullet points to
   capture definitions, key ideas, examples, and questions in your own words.
   After class, close your notes and practise active recall: reconstruct the
   main ideas from memory, then reopen the notebook to identify what you
   missed or misunderstood. If you discover a gap, ask your classmates and
   compare notes; they are part of your learning community and may well become
   lifelong friends. If the point remains unclear, bring the question to me
   during consultation hours.

   ::: {.callout-note title="Use of generative AI"}
   I strongly encourage the cautious use of generative-AI tools—including
   ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and similar systems—for self-study. They
   can help you request another explanation, generate practice questions, or
   explore a topic from a different angle. However, they can also produce
   convincing but incorrect answers, so check their claims against the course
   notes and work through the mathematics yourself.

   Do not become dependent on these tools. They will not be available to help
   you in real time during graded assessments, where you must explain and apply
   ideas independently. All quizzes and recitations will be announced in
   advance and completed in class; there will be no take-home quizzes or
   recitations.
   :::

7. **Work steadily, but keep marks in perspective.** I recognise that we are
   working within a tight academic schedule, so assessments will be designed
   deliberately and kept proportionate to the time and material available.
   Your marks will reflect the published assessment criteria and the work you
   submit.

   Examinations will not contain “curveball” questions based on material whose
   status has been left unclear. We may occasionally discuss an interesting
   idea beyond the essential course content; when we do, I will state
   explicitly whether it is examinable or non-examinable. This follows the
   transparent approach to assessment that I encountered in British
   universities. An examination may still ask you to apply a familiar idea in
   a new setting, but it will not quietly test a topic that was presented as
   optional enrichment.

   ::: {.callout-note title="A sidenote on our Lingua Franca"}
   You may also notice an occasional mixture of British and American English
   in these notes. My basic education used American English, whereas my
   university education used British English, and I still move between the two
   conventions. I apologise for any resulting inconsistency; it should never
   affect the mathematical meaning. Students may use either convention—the
   important things are clarity and consistency.

   I encourage everyone to practise using English because it is the principal
   language of much of the biology literature you will encounter. This is an
   encouragement, not a barrier to participation: English, Tagalog, and
   Cebuano are all welcome in class, and no one will be treated differently
   for choosing among them. I am open to questions in other languages as well,
   although I may need you or a classmate to translate if I do not understand
   them. If you find my accent or English difficult to follow, please tell me,
   either during class or privately. I can explain in Taglish whenever
   practicable while retaining the technical terms needed for the subject.
   :::

   Rather than worrying constantly about individual scores, focus on sustained
   effort, academic discipline, and responding constructively to feedback. If
   you do those things consistently, there should be no unpleasant surprises
   when you receive your class card. You have earned your place among
   Bulacan's capable and hardworking students. Have faith in your ability—I
   have faith in you, too.

8. **Read the course notes before class.** Since this is my first time teaching
   this course, the complete collection of lecture notes is still under
   construction. However, I will make the notes for each day's scheduled
   topics available at least two weeks before we cover them.

   You are not expected to master the material before the lecture. The aim is
   simply to make an initial acquaintance with it: skim the headings, notice
   the main definitions and examples, and identify anything that already
   raises a question. Even a brief preview will make the topic feel less
   unfamiliar and help you follow the discussion without feeling lost.

   Much of our fear of mathematics is learned through discouraging experiences
   and the widespread assumption that only a few people can understand it.
   Mathematics can certainly be difficult, but it is not uniquely so: biology,
   economics, chemistry, and every other serious discipline present their own
   unfamiliar ideas and ways of thinking. As the course progresses, I hope you
   will discover that mathematics becomes approachable when it is explained
   patiently, connected to meaningful problems, and studied consistently.

9. **Correct mistakes—respectfully.** I strongly encourage you to point out
   errors, whether they appear in the notes, in a classmate's reasoning, or in
   something I have said or written. Corrections should address the idea rather
   than embarrass the person, and this is especially important when correcting
   one another.

   If the mistake is mine, please do not hesitate to say so. Valid corrections
   of mathematical or factual errors in my lectures or course materials may
   earn extra credit, under the same criteria and opportunity available to
   everyone. I am thoroughly egalitarian about this: finding something I have
   got wrong is not a challenge to my authority. My reaction will be unabated
   delight, because careful criticism improves both the notes and the class.

10. **Ask for help when you are struggling.** You will not be judged for finding
   something difficult or for admitting that you do not yet understand it. I
   struggled in several classes when I was a student, too, and I made progress
   by seeking guidance rather than insisting that I solve every difficulty
   alone. You are part of a wider BulSU community that can support your
   learning. Your teacher should be one of the first people you can approach,
   and in this course, that person is me.
